About: Polarization & Malus's Law

Source

Topic
Wave optics — polarization of transverse EM waves
Concept
Unpolarized light loses exactly half its intensity at its first polarizer, whatever the axis; a second polarizer at angle θ then transmits I·cos²θ.
Serves
Distinguishing the FIRST filter (unpolarized → polarized, factor ½) from every subsequent filter (Malus's law).

Guided Inquiry

1 · The apparatus

A source emits light of intensity I₀ whose electric field points in every direction perpendicular to the beam, with equal likelihood. Two polarizing filters follow, P₁ with its transmission axis at θ₁ and P₂ at θ₂, and a screen collects whatever gets through.

A filter passes only the component of the electric field that lies along its own transmission axis.

2 · The first filter

Unpolarized light of intensity I₀ meets P₁, whose axis is at θ₁. What intensity emerges?

3 · A second filter, crossed

P₂ is now set perpendicular to P₁. What reaches the screen?

4 · Turning the analyser

Turn the P₂ axis from 0° to 90° and compare the screen at Δθ = 0°, 45°, 60° and 90° against I₁ = 0.500.

That dependence, I₂ = I₁·cos²(Δθ), is Malus's law.

5 · A third filter between the crossed pair

P₁ and P₂ are crossed and the screen is dark. A third filter P₃ is slid in between them, with its axis at 45° to both. What now reaches the screen?

6 · Three filters, three stages

The chain now reads I₃ = ½I₀·cos²(θ₃−θ₁) and I₂ = I₃·cos²(θ₂−θ₃): one factor of ½ at the unpolarized input, then one Malus factor per filter after it.

Turn θ₃ across its range and watch the screen; θ₁ and θ₂ stay crossed.

First filter: unpolarized → polarized, factor ½. Every next filter: Malus, cos²(Δθ). Per-stage intensities I₀, I₁, I₂ (and I₃ when the middle filter is on) are labelled on the apparatus.
First filter — unpolarized input
Averaging cos²θ over all incident directions gives ½. The output is polarized along P₁'s axis whatever went in.
Malus's law — polarized input
Δθ is measured between the incoming polarization axis and the next filter's transmission axis.
Two-polarizer chain
Crossed (Δθ = 90°) ⇒ 0. Parallel (Δθ = 0) ⇒ I₀/2.
Three-polarizer chain
Even with P₁ ⟂ P₂, inserting a middle filter at 45° gives I₀/8 on the screen — the classic paradox.

01

At a glance

A lamp sends light through up to three polarizing filters, and a screen at the end shows how much of it arrives. Turning the filters and watching the screen lets you work out the rule that sets the brightness.

What you'll learn

  • What a polarizing filter does to the electric field of light, and why its axis angle matters.
  • How the intensity changes at the first filter and at each filter after it.
  • What happens to the screen when a third filter is placed between two others.
Light from the source meets P₁, then P₂, then the screen. The dashed lines are the transmission axes. A third filter can be slid in between.

What's on screen

  • Filters P₁, P₂, P₃: slotted disks, each with a dashed axis line and an axis … ° label.
  • Beam arrows: the electric field, drawn in the plane across the beam. Their length follows the amplitude.
  • Numbers: I₀ under the source, I = under each filter, and I₂ with its percentage of I₀ under the screen.
  • Screen: its brightness follows the intensity that reaches it.
See itStart with P₁ at 0° and P₂ at 45°, and no third filter. Watch for: the arrows turning from random directions to one direction at P₁, and the screen glowing.

03

The first filter passes half of an unpolarized beam

Light is a transverse wave: its electric field points across the beam. In unpolarized light that direction is random and every direction is equally likely. A filter passes only the part of the field along its transmission axis. A field at angle θ to the axis has a share cos²θ of its intensity along it.

Averaged over all directions, cos²θ is ½. So the first filter always passes half the intensity, whatever θ₁ is:

I1 = ½ I0
Same for every axis angle θ₁.

What leaves P₁ is polarized: its field points along P₁'s axis. Turning P₁ turns that direction and does not change the amount.

See itTurn P₁ to 60° with I₀ = 1. Watch for: I = 0.500 under P₁, the same as at 0°, while the arrows after it lean with the new axis.
04

Malus's law sets what each later filter passes

Light that is already polarized has one field direction. A filter whose axis is at angle Δθ to it passes the field component E cos Δθ. Intensity goes as the square of the field, so

Iout = Iin cos²Δθ
Malus's law. Δθ is the angle between the incoming polarization and the filter's axis.

With two filters, I₂ = ½ I₀ cos²(θ₂ − θ₁). Only the difference matters. Parallel axes pass everything that P₁ let through, and crossed axes (Δθ = 90°) pass nothing. With I₀ = 1:

Δθcos²ΔθI₂
0°10.500
30°0.750.375
45°0.500.250
60°0.250.125
90°00
See itPut P₂ at 60° from P₁, with no third filter. Watch for: the screen reading I₂ = 0.125, which is 12.5% of I₀, a quarter of the 0.500 that left P₁.
05

A filter between a crossed pair lets light through

With P₁ and P₂ crossed, the light leaving P₁ has no field along P₂'s axis, so the screen is dark. Now slide P₃ in between, with its axis at 45° to both.

  • P₁ passes ½ of I₀.
  • P₃ is 45° from P₁'s polarization, so it passes cos²45° = ½ of that, and the light leaves polarized along P₃'s axis.
  • P₂ is 45° from P₃'s axis, so it passes another ½.

The screen gets ½ × ½ × ½ = ⅛ of I₀. A filter does not only remove light. It sets a new polarization direction, and the next filter measures its angle from that new direction. Take P₃ out and the screen goes dark again.

See itCross P₁ (0°) and P₂ (90°), then put P₃ in at 45°. Watch for: the screen lighting up to I₂ = 0.125, and Δθ reading 45°, 45°.
06

The middle filter's angle sets the brightness

Each filter after the first multiplies the intensity by cos² of its own angle step:

I2 = ½ I0 cos²(θ3 − θ1) cos²(θ2 − θ3)
One factor ½ for the unpolarized input, then one Malus factor per filter.

With P₁ at 0° and P₂ at 90°, this becomes (I₀/8) sin²(2θ₃). It peaks at θ₃ = 45° with I₀/8, and falls to zero at 0° and 90°, where P₃ lines up with one filter and is crossed with the other. A negative θ₃ gives the same result as the matching positive one.

Read from the sim's own controls.

See itKeep P₁ at 0° and P₂ at 90°, and turn P₃ to 30°. Watch for: I₂ = 0.094 (9.4% of I₀), dimmer than the 12.5% at 45°.
07

Where it matters

  • Sunglasses. Light reflected from water or a road is partly polarized along the surface. Polarizing lenses with their axis set across that direction cut the glare.
  • Camera filters. Light from a clear blue sky is partly polarized, so rotating a polarizing filter on a lens darkens the sky and lets you remove reflections.
  • LCD screens. Each pixel sits between two polarizing sheets. A liquid-crystal layer turns the light's polarization, which sets how much passes the second sheet.
08

Summary

In one line. A polarizing filter passes only the part of the light's electric field that lies along its axis, so the screen's brightness depends on the angles between the filters.

Key points

  • Unpolarized light loses half its intensity at the first filter, whatever its axis: I₁ = ½ I₀.
  • Each later filter gives Iout = Iin cos²Δθ, with Δθ measured from the direction the light now has.
  • A middle filter at 45° between crossed filters lets I₀/8 through.

Common mix-ups

  • "The first filter passes cos²θ₁ of the beam." The beam has no single direction yet, so the first filter passes half of it for every θ₁. Malus's law applies from the second filter on.
  • "Extra filters can only make the screen dimmer." Between a crossed pair, a third filter takes the screen from dark to I₀/8, because it turns the polarization.
  • "Crossed filters stop light because they absorb everything." Each one is fine alone. The light from P₁ simply has no field along P₂'s axis.

Things to try on your own

  • Set θ₁ = −30° and θ₂ = 30° with P₃ out, and predict I₂ before reading it.
  • With P₁ at 0° and P₂ at 90°, find two θ₃ values that give the same screen brightness.
  • Find the θ₃ that gives the brightest screen when P₁ is at 0° and P₂ is at 60°.
